## The big idea

Nobody derives a real pump curve — too much geometry, too much turbulence.
The manufacturer **measures one machine once**, and then dimensional analysis
does what it always does in this course: it stretches a single measurement
across an entire family. The affinity laws ($Q \propto \omega$,
$H \propto \omega^2$, $P \propto \omega^3$) are pump scaling; and collapsing
the family's whole résumé into one number gives the **specific speed** — the
dimensionless name for the machine's *shape*. Unit 2 promised that the
dimensionless number tells you which physics is in charge. Here it goes one
better: it tells you which machine to buy.

::: {.callout-note}
### The number in charge: specific speed
$$N_s = \frac{\omega\,\sqrt{Q}}{(gH)^{3/4}}$$
evaluated at the best-efficiency point. Low $N_s$ (≲ 1.5): radial impeller —
modest flow squeezed to high head. High $N_s$ (≳ 3.5): axial propeller — a
river moved gently. Between: mixed-flow. The duty picks the number; the
number picks the machine; the engineer signs the purchase order.
:::

## One measurement, a whole family

Run Buckingham on a pump. What matters: flow $Q$, head (as energy per mass,
$gH$), power $P$, speed $\omega$, size $D$, density $\rho$ (viscosity sits
this one out at industrial Reynolds numbers — the regime argument of Unit 2,
deployed). Six variables, three dimensions, three groups:

$$C_Q = \frac{Q}{\omega D^3}, \qquad
C_H = \frac{gH}{\omega^2 D^2}, \qquad
C_P = \frac{P}{\rho\, \omega^3 D^5}.$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Click for where the affinity laws come from
Geometrically similar pumps running at the same $C_Q$ are *dynamically
similar* — same velocity triangles, just rescaled (module 10.1's triangles,
literally stretched). So they share their values of $C_H$ and $C_P$: a
pump family is **one curve** in $(C_Q, C_H)$ space, exactly as all spheres
were one curve in $(Re, C_D)$ space. Now hold $D$ fixed (same machine, new
speed) and keep $C_Q$ constant: $Q \propto \omega$. Constant $C_H$:
$H \propto \omega^2$. Constant $C_P$: $P \propto \omega^3$. That's the
whole derivation — the affinity laws are Buckingham wearing a hard hat.
:::

Same machine, new speed $\omega' = k\,\omega$: every point of the measured
curve moves by

$$Q' = kQ, \qquad H' = k^2 H, \qquad P' = k^3 P.$$

That last exponent is where the money is. Slowing a pump (or fan) to 80%
speed costs you 20% of the flow and **half the power** ($0.8^3 = 0.51$).
The alternative — throttling — keeps the motor near full song and burns the
difference across a valve. This is why variable-frequency drives pay for
themselves with almost indecent speed on any pump that spends its life at
part load, and why "we'll just pinch the discharge valve" is a sentence that
should cost the speaker a coffee.[^trim]

[^trim]: The poor-man's speed change is *trimming* — machining the impeller
down a few percent. Over small changes it obeys nearly the same laws
(`Pump.trimmed()` in the toolbox). It's cheap, permanent, and you can't
untrim; measure twice.

## The number that names the machine

The three coefficients describe a family; to *choose* a family, eliminate
the size. Combine $C_Q$ and $C_H$ so that $D$ cancels:

$$N_s = \frac{C_Q^{1/2}}{C_H^{3/4}} = \frac{\omega \sqrt{Q}}{(gH)^{3/4}},$$

evaluated at the BEP. It is a pure number (radians being nobody's unit), and
it sorts the entire catalog:[^us] a duty of huge head and polite flow gives a
small $N_s$ — a radial impeller, all centrifugal squeeze; huge flow over a
levee's worth of head gives a large $N_s$ — an axial propeller, all
throughput. Between them, mixed-flow machines fill the gap. Fighting the
habitat — asking a radial machine to gulp a river, or a propeller to feed a
boiler — buys you an efficiency in the basement and a vibration signature
your maintenance crew will learn to dread. The shape is not negotiable; the
duty already chose it.

[^us]: US catalogs quote $N_s = \text{rpm}\sqrt{\text{gpm}}/H_\text{ft}^{3/4}$
— same idea wearing dimensional clothes (Unit 2's suspicious constant,
spotted in the wild again). The toolbox speaks both: `specific_speed()` and
`specific_speed_US()`.

::: {.column-margin}
Efficiency also cares how *big* the machine is — a 5 MW pump laughs at
leakage and surface-finish losses that gnaw a 5 kW one. Similarity gets you
to the neighborhood; the catalog's measured efficiency islands take you to
the door.
:::

## Play with it

A pump measured at 1750 rpm ($H = 40 - 9\times10^4\,Q^2$) feeds the module
8.4 tank system. You now own a VFD. Slide the speed; the whole measured
curve obeys the affinity laws, and the operating point — with its power
bill — follows.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof k_102 = Inputs.range([0.5, 1.2], {value: 1.0, step: 0.05, label: "speed ratio ω′/ω"})
viewof z2_102 = Inputs.range([0, 30], {value: 12, step: 2, label: "tank elevation z₂ (m)"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - k_102
#|   - z2_102
w = water(20)
base = Pump.from_coeffs(h0=40, a=9e4, efficiency=0.70)
pump = base.at_speed(k_102)

sys = PipeSystem(fluid=w, z1=0, z2=z2_102)
sys.add(Pipe(L=60, D=0.080, roughness='commercial_steel'))
sys.add(pump)

Qs = np.linspace(1e-6, 0.026, 140)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.6))
ax.plot(Qs*1000, [base.head(q) for q in Qs], lw=1.5, color='gray', ls=':',
        label='measured curve (1750 rpm)')
ax.plot(Qs*1000, [pump.head(q) for q in Qs], lw=2.5, color='crimson',
        label=f'affinity-scaled ({k_102:.2f}× speed)')
ax.plot(Qs*1000, [sys.static_head() + sys.head_loss(q) for q in Qs],
        lw=2.5, color='steelblue', label='flow curve')
try:
    Qop = sys.solve_flow()
    Hop = pump.head(Qop)
    P = w.rho * 9.81 * Qop * Hop / 0.70
    ax.plot(Qop*1000, Hop, 'o', ms=12, mfc='gold', mec='k', zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(f"  {Qop*1000:.1f} L/s at {Hop:.1f} m\n  shaft ≈ {P/1000:.2f} kW"
                f"  (∝ speed³: {k_102**3:.2f}× of full-speed scale)",
                (Qop*1000, Hop), fontsize=9)
    ax.set_title("the curve moves as a family: Q by k, H by k², P by k³")
except Exception:
    ax.set_title("no crossing: the slowed pump can no longer clear the static head")
ax.set_xlabel('Q (L/s)'); ax.set_ylabel('head (m)')
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_ylim(0, 62)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Two experiments. **Ease the speed down** with the tank at 12 m and watch the
power annotation fall like $k^3$ — then keep going and find the speed where
the curves stop crossing entirely: static head doesn't scale down with your
motor, and it will happily strand a too-slow pump (shutoff head $\propto
k^2$ eventually ducks under $z_2$). **Raise the tank** and repeat: the more
static-dominated the system, the *less* turndown room a VFD has. Speed
control is glorious against friction and merely mortal against gravity.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
"Buy the bigger pump to be safe." Safety, here, is a place on the curve, not
a size. An oversized machine runs far left of its BEP: efficiency down,
radial loads and vibration up, recirculation gnawing at the impeller eye,
and — the sting — a *higher* NPSH appetite right where the suction line is
weakest. Right-sizing isn't frugality; it's mechanical kindness.
:::

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** A cooling loop runs 24/7 and needs full flow only 10% of the time; 70% flow covers the rest. Estimate the energy saving of a VFD versus throttling for the 90% of hours at reduced load.</summary>
At 70% speed the pump draws $0.7^3 \approx 34\%$ of full power. Throttling
to the same flow keeps the machine near full head and typically 80–90% of
full power. Saving ≈ 50 percentage points of the pump's rating for 90% of
the year — this is why VFD retrofits are often the plant engineer's easiest
budget win. (Homework prices a real one.)
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Duty: 0.03 m³/s against 25 m at 1750 rpm. Compute $N_s$ and name the machine.</summary>
$\omega = 183$ rad/s, so $N_s = 183\sqrt{0.03}/(9.81\cdot25)^{3/4} \approx
0.51$ — deep in radial-centrifugal country (`classify_pump(0.51)` agrees).
A propeller pump at this duty would be a very expensive noise generator.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** Why is a pump's *measured* curve at one speed enough to design with at any nearby speed — and what quietly guaranteed it?</summary>
Affinity: the machine stays geometrically identical, so equal $C_Q$ means
similar velocity triangles and equal $C_H$, $C_P$. One curve in coefficient
space *is* every speed's curve. The guarantee is dynamic similarity — the
same logic that let one sphere test stand for all spheres in Unit 2. The
course thesis, now with a purchase order attached.
</details>
